This game actually feels like you're playing to the rhythm instead of spamming dense notes at a high speed. The official levels are well made and fun, the level editor is very advanced which allows for some really in-depth creativity, and the game is simply very satisfying to play.

My biggest complaint however, is how unforgiving the game is. It becomes very difficult to improve at this game because you only get one try to complete the song. This prevents you from easily practicing specific patterns you struggle on. It shares some similarities with games like Geometry Dash where you mess up once and it's over, the major difference though is this game does not include a dedicated practice mode. I really would prefer there to be some way to practice levels outside of the editor which actually allows you to miss beats and continue.

+ The game is unique
+ The game is super satisfying to play
+ The menu is creative
+ The editor allows creators to put in a lot of detail

- The game has a very difficult learning curve
- The game doesn't explain a lot of things to you
- The game prevents you from improving with the lack of a practice mode

In the game dance of fire and ice, you play the red and blue circles that rotate around and move around to other side until the last square with a white circle. You have to press the space bar key or mouse to fit the timing of the circle going into the square-shaped compartment and the timing is organized to suit the background music. As the chapter goes up the rhythm of the beat, the treadmill, the notes, and so on become more complicated. the ruling is generous, but it must proceed immediately without a break, and if it misses, it must start all over again, requiring enough concentration to clear up at once.

[h1] Here are some Impressions and thoughts about the game [/h1]

- It's way less demanding spec wise for my potato pc which is always a nice bonus :D

- Developers are 7th Beat Games and also planning to release another game called Rhythm Doctor coming out in 2019
You can play the demo of Rhythm Doctor here : http://rhythmdr.com/

- Unique, refreshing, and a hidden gem game of the rhythm music genre with nice use of geometry and visual effects. 

- I like that they have mini-tutorials showing the beats and how it's going to be in general of the level

- I'm not sure if it's called latency? but it detects your lag and sets the appropriate timing of the circles touching the tile which I appreciate it :)

- This game is one of the reasons I crave for rhythm games with the flow after have been playing Audiosurf game. It made my heart beat again tuning along its fun musical journey :)

- I love that all the music makes you feel like you are playing an instrument. Such as trumpet, drum, piano, triangle, female vocal and so on. 

- Simple mechanic, challenging and difficult to master. (If you are good at Osu! or any rhythm games it might be easier to beat)

- Price wise it is very affordable and worth every penny.

- It can be challenging but rewarding to finish. I'm almost new to this genre of game so it took me some tries to finish a few levels.

- I was a little annoyed at times and needed to have a break due to being tired out of failing repeatedly at the same spot of the end part.

- I'm glad that the developers are adding more worlds without any DLC that needs to be paid.

- The scenery matches the concept and vibe of the music.

- Pace wise some levels feel like you are walking, jogging, and running. 

- You kind of have to guess or memorize the beats at times but don't worry the tutorial lets you get the feel of how it's going to be like.

- I love that music is unique and versatile. It feels like I'm really in a zone with the different themed world. Some music makes me feel like I'm in trance, some with jazzy flow, metal, electronic, and Latin style. Nice mix of upbeat and mellow sounds.

[h1] Some Suggestions & Ideas [/h1]

- Having story mode with musical bosses 

- Background/music/tiles workshop made by players

- Being able to play custom music and backgrounds and the tile automatically set with the beat of the music would be neat.

- I wish there is a cosmetic item for the red and blue balls like different colors, patterns, shapes, and designs.

- It would be also interesting if there is multiplayer where they take blue or red and then work together. Competitive mode would be interesting too.

- I wish there is a slow-paced mode because I'm one of the slow reaction kind of person and just want to relax and enjoy.

- The tiles can be a bit bright for people sensitive with lights so I wish there is an option to make it set low or turn off for easy on eyes.

- Using voice for control would be neat. When I was playing this, I was always humming the beats and tapping my fingers and toes :D

In conclusion, this game may look like your average rhythm game but have more depth and can be challenging in a refreshing way. If you like a music rhythm game with using one button control, less relaxing (one that keeps you on your toes), like aiming for perfection with no mistakes I suggest give it a try and support them to make more new games :D It also helps you practice skill of your sense of reaction and endurance. If you are impatient, don't like having to start the level again when making single mistake, don't like doing finger exercise, prefer custom music and pace, have a sloth like reaction, you might get a bit annoyed mainly due to it's difficulty and game mechanic.

Just yesterday I got the last few achievements I needed in this game. Today I open the game and all of my save data is gone. 200 hours of my life, down the drain, because of Steam's shitty cloud save system. Because I'll likely never be willing to put in that time again, I felt like writing this review as a final goodbye to the game.

A Dance of Fire and Ice is a very refreshing rhythm game. As someone who has been interested in music for a few years now, the way the game visualizes various elements of rhythm is genius. I absolutely love the 13 main levels. The mechanics introduced in them mostly centers around the concepts getting increasingly janky. Pulse is the first level that kicks off that trend by using a very strange time signature, and forcing the player to go with it. Jungle City (level 8) introduces triplets, and from there, more and more rhythmic concepts are introduced that make completing a stage all the more fun. However, if you decide you're up for a bit more of a challenge, look no further than B-X. It's a bonus stage that acts as a sort of "final challenge" for people who really want it. It's tough, I'd be willing to bet it's where the majority of those 200+ hours came from, but it can be bested. Now, the extra levels. Getting the negatives out of the way, I don't like how some of them are borderline unreadable, and rely on exclusively muscle memory, but other than that, I adore these levels. They each introduce a new, cool mechanic that expands on the game. There are two more bonus levels that are unlocked when you beat B-X, but I didn't get the chance to mess around with them before my data was wiped, so I can't give an opinion on them. I also never messed around with the level editor all that much, either. Overall, I would more than recommend this game to anyone who likes rhythm games. The only criticism I would have with the game as a whole would be that nowhere in the game does it recommend you use your keyboard. I beat every level up to Jungle City using just my mouse, and it was very painful. If you are on the edge about buying this niche little indie game, and my stupid review is somehow the deciding factor for whether you buy it or not, I'd say to at least try it out. For being only a few bucks, you get infinitely more than you pay for in my opinion. I love this game, but I'm not sure I'll ever come back to it, with my 200+ hours of progress getting erased and all. 

8/10, worth every penny.

ADOFAI (A Dance Of Fire And Ice) has one of the simpler premises i've seen for rhythm games. It's fun and addicting at first, but gets frustrating quickly.

My main issue with ADOFAI is the fact that it seems to restrict mappers in the maps they can create, thus limiting the fun that can be had. If a song has one main lead to follow, or pattern that it always has, this game works wonders. But as soon as a song switches focus, or a mapper wants to focus on a new pattern in the song, it quickly falls apart. There seems to be no transition block (or note, whatevs) that allows for smooth transitions between patterns, which leads to a miss. There also lies my second issue with the game.

Because of the way ADOFAI is structured, missing a note is critical. More-so than with other games like guitar hero or osu!, because here, a miss means you are DEAD, no second chances. This makes improving at ADOFAI very difficult and in my opinion, very frustrating to play.
"Oh, you got though 80% of the map? Well I'm switching patterns now, so better be prepared to hit this note where for which there are no reasons to believe i should be here beforehand." 

This type of game really favors people who keep playing one map over and over again, (boring, imo) instead of people who like playing a wide range of maps and listen to many different songs. (imo, fun)

That brings me to my third point, and my point that doesn't just affect ADOFAI, but other rhythm games as well such as Beat Saber; the lack of (good) maps, or even worse in ADOFAI's case, song variety. In ADOFAI, you are limited strictly to the songs artists have given explicit permission to use for ADOFAI, unlike games like osu! or Beat Saber. This makes it so the choice of songs mappers can well, map, is much, MUCH stricter than usual, and the outcome is even less maps. This makes improvement much harder since the maps that are available will have higher skill gaps between maps than games with many maps and songs.


Now because i do realize that this review is all over the place here is the TL;DR:
The good:
1) The songs that are in the "worlds" that come with the game are well mapped and fun to play
2) You can download more maps from the workshop (ill get to this in the bad as well)

The bad:
1) The very strict note hitting makes the game frustrating to play, because one miss means you are dead. This makes point two so much worse.
2) There are no smooth transitions between patterns in music, which makes it very easy to miss when the song changes a pattern or lead.
3) There are not that many (good) maps that you can choose from, making improvement more difficult.
4) Bad song variety. ADOFAI mappers are limited to artists that have given approval for their songs to be used in ADOFAI. Do you want to play a song by, lets say, Pendulum? (D&B artist) Well too bad, he didnt give permission for his songs to be used in ADOFAI, so you can't play them.

Overall: Can be fun, but it's just not for me past the built in worlds.

Edit: I do think it should be added that this is what some people really enjoy, the insane difficulty, the hard songs, the steep learning curve of weird patterns, etc. It's just not for me.

A fantastic rhythm game experience. One of the things I was most worried about when purchasing this game was that it would eventually prove too difficult for me to beat. I consider myself great at most games, though rhythm games that require fast tapping are not my forte. This game is nice enough to give you a difficulty slope that you can climb up slowly; levels start out extremely easy and gradually use more and more difficult patterns, but never reach the point where they are unbeatable.

In terms of content, there are [spoiler] 12 [/spoiler] main levels, a bonus level, a selection of [i]Muse Dash[/i] levels, and a selection of developer's choice community levels, as well as a separate community level creator/browser where you can create or play custom levels. I'm going to focus on the main levels, since I haven't played any of the special content. Each of the main levels gives you several short tutorials before you end up playing the level itself; these serve to teach you some mechanics that will appear in the level that would otherwise throw you off. You can also practice any level on the fly, though you can only practice from the beginning of the level to slightly past your furthest attempt. Each level also has a speed challenge where you are required to beat the level at a faster pace, though you can slowly bump up the speed to make the transition to the goal speed easier.

I mentioned difficulty before; each level is fair and fun, with levels becoming increasingly difficult as you progress. If you consider yourself good at most games, you shouldn't have much of a challenge beating the main levels, though some speed challenges may prove difficult. The bonus level in particular is the fastest and most difficult level in the main game, though it is only required if you plan on getting all of the achievements. There is a bit of artificial difficulty that stems from the visual effects that some levels have, though they are never overbearing, and you end up getting used to them. The developers seemed to want the game to be more of a fun, engaging experience rather than a hardcore rhythm game for [i]Osu![/i] professionals, which I personally appreciate. I enjoyed every one of the main levels. [spoiler] Except for the Jungle City speed challenge. That shit blows. [/spoiler]

All in all, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for a new game to scratch that rhythm itch. If you're looking for casual fun, most of the levels will suit your needs. If you're looking for a brutally difficult challenge, the speed challenges, special levels, and community levels fit that definition. Or if you're like me and you're just looking for an equally fun/challenging rhythm game, you've come to the right place.

A Dance of Fire and Ice is a strict rhythm game which promotes the player to not make mistakes, learn patterns and rhythms in songs, and to experience challenging but rewarding gameplay. This means that if you are buying this game, keep in mind: THIS GAME IS NOT GOING TO BE A CASUAL EXPERIENCE, IT REQUIRES FOCUS AND DETERMINATION IN ORDER TO COMPLETE MOST SONGS. Having gotten past that point, I will discuss how this gameplay FEELS in my personal playing of the game, and explain important points that YOU should keep in mind when buying the game. 

In the game, you are given 12 main worlds to play, along with 8 "extra" worlds. All of these worlds are unique in their own way, each promoting a different use of musical style, patterns, and difficulty. The first worlds begin with very basic rhythms and beats, which anybody can learn and play, but the later worlds progress into more complex rhythms which can confuse the typical human mind. The diversity in music and rhythms allows for gameplay which promotes you to use your mind to find patterns in the music, and to draw connections to them with the overall beat. This can lead to very challenging but incredibly rewarding gameplay.

The gameplay itself is very boss-like in nature, with each map being designed as if you are training to fight the boss. Each map features multiple sections where you play excerpts that feature a specific pattern or rhythm of that song, then once you've learned each one and passed their tests, you take on the final trial. This makes the game feel AMAZING when you accomplish learning these rhythms and patterns, and gives you a great feeling of success when you pass the full puzzle. (Just like a boss battle with it's minions leading up to it.) This can result in some levels being much harder than others, as the patterns can be more wild and difficult to understand, but eventually being able to overcome those difficulties and achieving a pass on that map with high accuracy is a very satisfying sensation.

The game does feature custom levels and the ability to create your own, which promotes replayability for people who have conquered the main and extra levels. There is limitations on what you can create, which unfortunately doesn't allow for there to be a massive load of maps such as there is in games like Osu!. But there is most certainly enough for you to enjoy yourself with for many of the well made custom levels, which can range heavily in difficulty. I am personally not a mapper, nor have tried extensively to create one, so I have no validation discussing anything related to the map editor and designer.

All of this combined creates an overall unique and special rhythm game experience, which can differ from person to person. When playing this game you must have the mindset that it will be a challenging battle on many of it's worlds, but when you complete those worlds with precision and accuracy you feel greatly rewarded and receive that fat dose of dopamine you were fighting for. Before you buy this game, keep in mind all of which has been discussed, and how you PERSONALLY would feel playing this game. I can surely tell you that I 100% got my money's worth out of this experience, and I am going to keep playing it for a good while.

I played the original game jam version of A Dance of Fire and Ice back in 2014, and it was one of the most unique rhythm game experiences that I've had. Fast-forward to 2019, I came across this and immediately bought it. Over the past nearly 2 years since this game's release, it's received many new levels, new mechanics, a level editor, and even steam workshop integration! It's crazy to see how much depth that the simple idea of "angle-based rhythms" had.

This game is all about recognizing patterns and being able to play out their rhythms. The beginning gameplay is very intuitive (though hard to grasp at first), where each world introduces new concepts in tutorial levels before finishing the world with a "boss song" to bring everything together. There are 12 "main" worlds that only barely scratch the surface. Once you complete those, there are several extra worlds with increasing difficulty, reaching a pinnacle of two "crown" worlds (at the time of review) that push far beyond the concepts introduced in the main worlds. After that, you can dive into the hundreds of custom levels with ever increasing difficulty. Even after playing this game for 450+ hours, there's still so much content left with the number of custom levels that the community creates daily.

All this for just $6.

A Dance of Fire and Ice, also known as ADOFAI, is a game that requires so much patience. When I originally bought the game, I had the mindset that since I had already been playing rhythm games for quite a long time the game would be pretty easy. Boy was I wrong about that assumption.

This game has such an amazing soundtrack filled with songs that can get you really hyped up and make you feel like you're about to accomplish something amazing. For me personally, World 11 was my favorite one. What is even better is that despite the game having an official soundtrack, they also made it so that you would be able to download and create charts for people to play! Because of this, the odds of getting bored because you "feel like you've done everything possible" is almost 0%.

Another thing that should be mentioned is the art. We all know those rhythm games like osu!, taiko, etc. that for the most part will have a still background. Not ADOFAI. No, this game has a background for each world that not only perfectly captures the mood that the song is going for, but also gives you something nice to look at. For example, in World 12, there is a part at the end that has several TV screens, one of which you are playing in. I can't say much more about it because of spoilers but that attention to detail just makes things so much more fun.

The other thing that I think I should really talk about is the overall difficulty of the game. This game can get incredibly hard but at the same time there are multiple worlds and charts that people have made that serve the purpose of letting you relax and maybe help relearn some of the basics. I also really enjoyed that before you were even allowed to try the last challenge of the world, you had to go through a unique tutorial for each world that taught you different things! 

In the end, I really do highly recommend this game to anyone who wants a fun little challenge. This is not a game to be underestimated due to how addicting it can get!

Incredible rhythm game.

You just need one button. (Theoretically.) The difficulty comes from reading. Unlike most rhythm games where notes come to you from one direction, here time travels in a circular motion. You tap when your orbiting planet aligns with the next tile. This alone makes the game so hard to read, but also so fun. You start to recognize certain patterns visually; for example, a square means two beats of double time, or an octagon means 3/4 beats.

The main levels give you plenty of tutorials. Most, if not all, patterns you'll see in the main song are taught through tutorials, so you can train yourself on each one. Which is a good thing: the main levels demand perfection. You cannot miss a single note, otherwise you have to restart -- sometimes from a checkpoint, but usually from the very beginning. It's tough, but the game gives you lots of ways to practice.

As a rhythm game, it also comes with its own level editor, with a vast amount of content. Many of them are published as featured levels in the game, so if you don't know where to look in the Workshop, just head to the featured section.

It's such a unique rhythm game, and I love unique mechanics like this. That's why it's an easy recommend. It's also very cheap for the amount of content it offers. You won't run out of stuff to play.

The game still has its ups and downs, such as freaking world 6, but it's still a lovely experience all around. Most definitely worth the $5.99 I paid for it and I even bought it for a friend who wanted it. The game shows you the almost endless possibilities presented to you with the level editor in the form of playable levels (which is kinda genius, honestly). I'm really looking forward to world 13. By the way, I can also proudly say that for someone who's been playing for 9 hours, I have beaten "Artificial Chariot" with a speed of 1.4x

Incredibly fun rhythm game that is sure to challenge players of all skill levels. While the game is fairly short, clocking in at around 90 minutes to beat total for me (this includes things like the [spoiler] speed modifiers and bonus level [/spoiler] which are extra content) it was no easy feat. For a rhythm game only featuring one button, there are some very tricky rhythms it pulls on the player to truly test their skill.

The only thing I'm slightly disappointed in is the lack of more complicated rhythms past worlds [spoiler]4 (best world, btw) and 5[/spoiler] but that may be remedied by future updates to the game adding more worlds to play.

At a price point of only $3, the game is definitely worth buying if you have an interest in rhythm games and challenging content.

If your looking for a fun and relaxing rhythm game then this isn't it. I have on several occasions wanted to delete myself when playing this game just because the developers put in songs and challenges that far outweigh the potential fun you could have. From worlds 1 - 8 I had a blast and starting to get the idea and pattern to some of the songs. But with the introduction with the last few worlds and the challenge levels, I have had my enjoyment and my life expectancy plummet. Am I subject to the idea of just "Git Gud"? Yes. I understand I can just sink even more time and pain into it to finally pass the level, but at what point does it just become a job? Complete it for just completions sake? I have several levels with 2000+ attempts just to beat the level and the time trial. I received all achievements and tried some of the new songs introduced in the update but I can't do it anymore. The game lost the fun and now it feels like a chore. I never play the game because I want to, but because the developers released a new song and "I guess I should beat it" This last one push me to leave this review and urge other rhythm game players to leave and try something else.
